cards.title: Perpendicular lines are two intersecting lines that meet at an exact right…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Perpendicular lines are two intersecting lines that meet at an exact right angle (90°). When line AB is perpendicular to line CD (written symbolically as AB ⊥ CD), all four angles formed at their point of intersection measure precisely 90°.
steps: Imagine walking into your classroom and looking at the corner where the walls meet the floor—the vertical wall and the horizontal floor form a square corner, which is a right angle!
In geometry, when two lines intersect to create this exact 90° square corner, we call them perpendicular lines.

To begin working with them, you must remember that intersecting lines form four angles around a central point, and if just one of those angles measures 90°, all adjacent and opposite angles must also equal 90°.

Building on your prior knowledge of basic angle types and intersecting lines from Class 6 geometry, you will now learn how to spot perpendicular indicators (like the square symbol at an intersection) and use them to…
The key insight is that perpendicularity is a special case of intersection where angles are locked at 90°.
cards.misconception: A poor answer simply states "draw it with a square tool" without explaining how to mathematically verify or construct a perpendicular line in an open field using numerical measurements.

cards.title: A transversal is a line that intersects two or more lines at distinct…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A transversal is a line that intersects two or more lines at distinct, separate points. When this third line crosses the others, it creates a rich geometric framework of eight distinct angles that allow us to study the relationship between lines.
steps: Imagine you are walking across a railway track where multiple parallel tracks run side by side, and a footpath crosses them diagonally at an angle.
The footpath is a line cutting across two or more other lines, creating a specific intersection pattern.
To begin studying this, we draw two lines on a paper and then draw a third line that crosses both of them.
We label the points where the third line meets the first two lines as our points of intersection.

cards.definition: The exterior angle property of a triangle states that if any side of a triangle is produced (extended), the exterior angle so formed is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles. This fundamental geometric rule allows us to find unknown angle measures in complex figures without needing to calculate all interior angles first.
steps: Imagine standing at the corner of a triangular park in your neighborhood, walking along one side, and then turning to continue along an extended path—the angle you turn through is the exterior angle!
To begin understanding this mathematically, draw any triangle on your paper and extend one of its sides outward with a straight line.
Recall from earlier work with lines and angles that a straight line measures 180 degrees, and triangles have an interior angle sum of 180 degrees.

By exploring how adjacent linear pairs relate to the remaining two angles inside the triangle, we discover a powerful shortcut: an exterior angle never depends on its adjacent interior neighbor, but always equals the…
This relationship forms a bridge between lines, angles, and algebraic equations.
remember: In triangle PQR, side QR is produced to point S, forming the exterior angle ∠ PRS. If the two interior opposite angles are ∠ P = 50° and ∠ Q = 60°, what is the measure of exterior….
Can an exterior angle of a triangle ever be smaller than one of its interior opposite angles? Explain why or why not using mathematical reasoning.
In ABC, side BC is extended to point D to form exterior angle ∠ ACD. If ∠ A = (3x + 10)°, ∠ B = (2x + 20)°, and exterior angle ∠ ACD = 120°, find the value of x.

cards.title: Constructing a triangle using the Side-Side-Side (SSS) criterion involves…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Constructing a triangle using the Side-Side-Side (SSS) criterion involves drawing a triangle when the exact lengths of all three of its sides are known, using a ruler and a pair of compasses. A unique triangle can be drawn if and only if the sum of the lengths of any two sides is strictly greater than the length of the third side (the Triangle Inequality Property).
steps: Imagine you are a carpenter in your village, and a client asks you to build a triangular wooden wall panel with exact side lengths of 7 cm, 5 cm, and 4 cm. How do you begin drawing this on a wooden board so that it fits…
You cannot just sketch it randomly; you need a precise geometric method starting with the longest side as your base line segment.
In Class 6, you learned how to construct simple line segments and basic angles using your ruler and compass.
Now, we will combine those tools to swing arcs that intersect at the exact third vertex, unlocking the secret of the SSS (Side-Side-Side) construction rule.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "a protractor" reveals a confusion between measuring angles and measuring/transferring linear side lengths, while an answer like "a set square" shows a lack of familiarity with standard geometric construction tools.
remember: What geometric tool is primarily used to measure and transfer an exact side length of a triangle from your ruler onto your construction paper when doing an SSS construction.
If you are given three side lengths of 3 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm, why is it impossible to construct a triangle using these lengths, even if you use a sharp pencil and precise compasses.
Construct a triangle PQR where side PQ = 6 cm, side QR = 5 cm, and side RP = 4 cm. What is the radius of the compass arc drawn from point P to locate vertex R.

cards.title: Constructing a triangle given two sides and the included angle (SAS) involves…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Constructing a triangle given two sides and the included angle (SAS) involves drawing a unique triangle using a ruler, compass, and protractor when the lengths of two sides and the measure of the angle formed between them are known. The "included angle" is strictly the angle positioned directly between the two given sides.
steps: Imagine you are a carpenter in your village tasked with building a triangular wooden frame for a decorative roof, and your client tells you two wooden beams must measure 6 cm and 8 cm, and the corner where they meet…
How do you start drawing this on paper before cutting the wood?
First, you draw the longer base line segment using your ruler to establish a firm foundation.
Next, you use your protractor at one end of the segment to measure and draw the given included angle precisely.
Finally, you measure off the second side length along that new angle ray using a compass, and connect the endpoints to complete the triangle.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer—such as believing it is any of the three angles in the triangle—reveals a failure to recognize that the angle must physically connect the two given sides for the construction to be uniquely determined.
remember: What does the term "included angle" mean when constructing a triangle using the SAS criterion.
If you are given side AB = 5 cm, side BC = 7 cm, and ∠ A = 50°, can you uniquely construct this triangle using the SAS method? Why or why not.
Describe the exact second step you must perform after drawing the first side segment XY = 6 cm when constructing XYZ with ∠ X = 60° and XZ = 8 cm.

cards.title: Multiplication of fractions is an operation where two or more fractional…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multiplication of fractions is an operation where two or more fractional numbers are combined by multiplying their numerators together to form the new numerator and their denominators together to form the new denominator. The fundamental rule states that for any fractions (a)/(b) and (c)/(d) where b ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0, the product is given by (a × c)/(b × d).
steps: Imagine you bought a large cake for your school farewell party, and after the party, (3)/(4) of the cake is left over.
The next day, your teacher asks you to take home (1)/(2) of that leftover cake.
How much of the whole original cake are you taking home?
To solve this, you need to find (1)/(2) of (3)/(4), which translates mathematically to multiplying (1)/(2) × (3)/(4).
Building on your prior knowledge of fractions as parts of a whole from Class 6, fraction multiplication represents finding a fractional part of another fractional quantity.
You begin by setting up the two fractions side by side with a multiplication sign between them.
remember: What is the primary rule for multiplying two fractions, such as (2)/(3) × (4)/(5).
Explain why multiplying two proper fractions (like (1)/(2) × (1)/(3)) results in a product that is smaller than either of the original fractions.
Calculate the product of (3)/(5) and (10)/(9), and write your answer in its simplest form.

cards.title: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number means finding a repeated sum or a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number means finding a repeated sum or a fractional part of that whole number, calculated by multiplying the whole number by the numerator and keeping the denominator the same. For any whole number w and fraction (a)/(b), the product is given by (w × a)/(b).
steps: Imagine you are buying 3 packets of biscuits, and each packet weighs (3)/(4) kg. To find the total weight, you need to add (3)/(4) three times: (3)/(4) + (3)/(4) + (3)/(4).
Just like repeated addition in whole numbers becomes multiplication (e.g., 3 × 4), repeated addition of fractions becomes multiplying a fraction by a whole number.
To begin, write down the whole number and the fraction as a multiplication expression: 3 × (3)/(4).
Connect this to what you learned in Class 6 about addition of like fractions.
The key insight is that the whole number multiplies only the numerator while the denominator remains unchanged.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like multiplying both numerator and denominator by the whole number reveals a confusion with creating equivalent fractions, where both terms are multiplied or divided by the same number.
remember: What is the rule for multiplying a whole number by a fraction (a)/(b).
Rahul says that 5 × (2)/(3) is equal to (10)/(15) because he multiplied both the top and bottom numbers by 5. Is Rahul correct? Explain why or why not.
Calculate the product of 6 and (4)/(9), and express your answer in its simplest form.

cards.title: Multiplying two fractions involves multiplying their numerators together to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multiplying two fractions involves multiplying their numerators together to form the new numerator and multiplying their denominators together to form the new denominator. The resulting fraction is then simplified to its lowest terms.
steps: Imagine you have a piece of cloth that is (3)/(4) of a metre long, and you need to use only (2)/(3) of that length for a craft project at school.
To find out what fraction of a whole metre you are actually using, you need to find a fraction of a fraction, which means multiplying the two fractions together.
To begin, write down the two fractions side by side with a multiplication sign between them, just like you did when multiplying whole numbers or integers.
Recall from earlier work that fractions represent parts of a whole, and multiplying them scales one part by another.

The key insight is the numerator and denominator rule: multiply the top numbers (numerators) together for the new top number, and multiply the bottom numbers (denominators) together for the new bottom number.
cards.misconception: A poor answer uses whole numbers only or fails to convert mixed fractions into improper fractions before multiplying.
remember: What is the rule for finding the numerator when multiplying two fractions together.
Explain why multiplying two proper fractions (like (1)/(2) × (1)/(2)) results in a product ((1)/(4)) that is smaller than either of the original fractions, unlike whole number….
Calculate the product of (3)/(5) and (4)/(7), and simplify if possible.

cards.title: The division of fractions using the reciprocal method is a rule where dividing…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The division of fractions using the reciprocal method is a rule where dividing any fraction by a non-zero fraction is performed by multiplying the first dividend fraction by the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of the second divisor fraction. Specifically, for any fractions (a)/(b) and (c)/(d) (where c, d ≠ 0), (a)/(b) ÷ (c)/(d) = (a)/(b) × (d)/(c) = (a × d)/(b × c).
steps: Imagine you have 3(1)/(2) litres of sweet buttermilk prepared for a school sports day party, and you want to pour it into small paper cups that each hold (1)/(4) of a litre.
How many cups can you fill completely?
To solve this, you need to divide the total quantity of buttermilk by the capacity of one cup, which means calculating 3(1)/(2) ÷ (1)/(4).

In Class 6, you learned how to multiply fractions by flipping factors and multiplying numerators and denominators, as well as visualizing fraction division as finding how many groups fit inside a total.

Today, we will expand that concept into a universal rule: instead of struggling with division directly, we transform division into multiplication by flipping the second fraction upside down—its reciprocal!
The key insight is that dividing by a fraction yields the exact same result as multiplying by its reciprocal.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like -(5)/(9) or (5)/(9) reveals that the student is confusing the reciprocal with the additive inverse (negative) or mistaking it for the original fraction itself, failing to understand that a reciprocal requires swapping the numerator and…
remember: What is the reciprocal of the fraction (5)/(9).
Explain why the operation of dividing by a fraction (3)/(4) is mathematically equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal (4)/(3).
Calculate the value of (7)/(8) ÷ (3)/(4) and express it in simplest form.

cards.title: Dividing a fraction by a whole number means partitioning a fractional quantity…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Dividing a fraction by a whole number means partitioning a fractional quantity into an equal number of whole parts, which is mathematically equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of that whole number.
steps: Imagine you have (3)/(4) of a large drum of drinking water left after a school camp, and you want to share it equally among 2 classrooms for watering plants.
How much of the total drum does each classroom get?
To solve this, we need to divide a fraction ((3)/(4)) by a whole number (2).
First, recall from Class 6 that a whole number like 2 can be written as a fraction with a denominator of 1, which is (2)/(1).
Next, apply the rule learned in fraction division: to divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
The reciprocal of (2)/(1) is (1)/(2).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like writing n itself reveals a failure to understand that the inverse of a whole number requires swapping its numerator and denominator (since n = (n)/(1)).
remember: What is the reciprocal of a whole number n (where n ≠ 0) when writing it as a fraction for division.
Explain why dividing a fraction (a)/(b) by a whole number c is the same as multiplying (a)/(b) by (1)/(c).
Calculate (5)/(8) ÷ 4 and write your answer in its simplest form.

cards.title: Dividing one fraction by another is the mathematical operation of finding how…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Dividing one fraction by another is the mathematical operation of finding how many times a second fraction (the divisor) fits into a first fraction (the dividend). This is computed by multiplying the dividend fraction by the reciprocal (inverse) of the divisor fraction.
steps: Imagine you have (3)/(4) of a litre of juice, and you want to pour it into smaller glasses that each hold (1)/(8) of a litre.
How many glasses can you fill?
To solve this, you need to find out how many groups of (1)/(8) fit into (3)/(4), which means dividing one fraction by another: (3)/(4) ÷ (1)/(8).
Just like in whole number division where dividing by a number is related to multiplying by its inverse, dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
The key insight is to change the division sign to multiplication and flip the second fraction upside down.
cards.misconception: A poor answer uses whole numbers disguised as fractions without demonstrating the core fraction operation.
remember: What is the reciprocal of the fraction (5)/(7).
Explain why we multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor when dividing two fractions instead of dividing the numerators and denominators directly.
Calculate the value of (3)/(5) ÷ (9)/(10) and write your answer in its simplest form.

cards.title: Solving word problems involving fraction multiplication requires translating…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Solving word problems involving fraction multiplication requires translating real-world scenarios into mathematical expressions where a fractional part of a quantity, fraction, or mixed number is computed by multiplying the numerators together and the denominators together.
steps: Imagine you went to the local vegetable market with your mother and bought 4 kilograms of potatoes, but you only used (3)/(4) of them to make evening snacks.
How do you find out the exact weight of the potatoes you used?
In Class 6, you learned how to multiply two fractions by multiplying numerators and denominators.
Now, in Class 7, we take that skill further by extracting mathematical clues from descriptive sentences to decide when and what to multiply.
The key insight is that the word "of" in mathematics almost always translates to multiplication (×), telling us we need to find a fraction of a given amount.
By identifying the total quantity and the fractional part taken, we set up our multiplication expression, simplify before multiplying, and attach the correct real-world unit to our final answer.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like addition or division shows the student does not understand that taking a fractional part ("(3)/(4) of the recipe") means multiplying the fraction by the total quantity required.
remember: A recipe calls for 2(1)/(2) cups of flour. If Rohan wants to make (3)/(4) of the recipe, what operation should he use to find the amount of flour needed, and why.

cards.title: Word problems involving fraction division require translating real-world…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Word problems involving fraction division require translating real-world scenarios of partitioning or sharing quantities into division expressions with fractions, and solving them using the reciprocal method. These problems typically ask how many portions of a given fractional size can be made from a total quantity, or what the whole quantity is given a fractional part.
steps: Imagine you bought 5(1)/(2) litres of paint to paint your school clubhouse, and each small container holds (3)/(4) of a litre.
How many containers can you fill?
To begin, you must read carefully to identify the total quantity available and the size of each part or group being created.
Next, translate this grouping scenario into a mathematical division statement: total quantity divided by the size of one part.
Connect this to your prior understanding of dividing one fraction by another by rewriting the division problem as multiplication by the reciprocal of the divisor.
Finally, compute the product, simplify the resulting fraction, and check your answer against the real-world context to see if it makes sense.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as multiplication or subtraction reveals that the student views fractions in word problems solely as keywords rather than visualizing partitioning a total length into equal-sized segments.
remember: If a tailor has a ribbon of length 3(1)/(2) metres and cuts it into pieces that are each (1)/(2) metre long, what mathematical operation should be used to find the total number of….

cards.title: The relationship between multiplication and division of fractions states that…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The relationship between multiplication and division of fractions states that dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse) of the divisor, meaning that if (a)/(b) ÷ (c)/(d) = e, then (a)/(b) = e × (c)/(d). This inverse relationship allows us to convert any fraction division problem into an equivalent multiplication problem.
steps: Imagine you bought 3(1)/(2) litres of paint and want to divide it equally into small containers that hold (1)/(2) litre each to share with your friends in your apartment building.
To find out how many containers you need, you perform a division: 3(1)/(2) ÷ (1)/(2).
But how can you check if your answer is correct using what you already know about multiplication?
Just like whole number division (12 ÷ 3 = 4 because 4 × 3 = 12), fraction division is completely undone by fraction multiplication.
We begin by converting mixed fractions to improper fractions and then observing how multiplying our quotient by the divisor brings us right back to our original dividend.
This connection shows that division is simply multiplication by the reciprocal!
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (such as "dividing by the reciprocal" or "multiplying by the same fraction") indicates the student confuses the definition of the reciprocal with regular operations and does not understand that division by a fraction transforms into…
remember: Which fraction operation is mathematically equivalent to dividing any number by a fraction (c)/(d).
If a student calculates (3)/(4) ÷ (2)/(5) = (15)/(8), how can they use multiplication to verify if their answer is correct.
Find the missing fraction x if x × (4)/(7) = (12)/(35).

cards.title: Simplifying complex fraction expressions involves reducing multi-layered or…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simplifying complex fraction expressions involves reducing multi-layered or compound fraction expressions—where numerators and denominators themselves contain fractions, sums, or products—into a single, simplest proper or improper fraction by systematically applying the order of operations and fractional division rules.
steps: Imagine you are helping at a school science fair in Delhi, and you need to divide a recipe of (3)/(4) litres of chemical solution equally among test tubes, but the measuring beaker itself has a fractional scale of…
When faced with a fraction divided by another fraction sitting inside a larger fraction bar, where do you even begin writing?
We begin by identifying the main fraction bar that separates the overall numerator from the overall denominator, treating the top and bottom expressions as separate mini-problems.
This builds directly upon our earlier skills of dividing fractions using reciprocals and finding common denominators for addition.
The key insight is to resolve the top and bottom completely into single fractions first, and then multiply the numerator by the reciprocal of the denominator.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer often shows the student adding or subtracting the denominators, or cross-multiplying the inner and outer numbers incorrectly, revealing a confusion between fraction division and fraction addition or cross-multiplication of proportions.
remember: What is the primary rule for simplifying a fraction expression where a fraction is divided by another fraction, such as ((a)/(b))/((c)/(d)).

cards.title: Congruent figures are geometric shapes that have the exact same shape and the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Congruent figures are geometric shapes that have the exact same shape and the exact same size, meaning one can be placed precisely over the other so that they cover each other completely through rigid transformations like translation, rotation, or reflection.
steps: Imagine you buy two identical brand-new exercise notebooks from a stationery shop in your market for ₹40 each.

When you stack them on top of your desk, the cover of the top book fits the bottom book so perfectly that no edges stick out. In geometry, when two objects match up completely in both shape and size, we call them…
Building on our earlier work with lines and basic shapes from Class 6, we now look closely at how geometric twins match identically.
To test if two figures are congruent, we can imagine lifting one figure and placing it onto the other—if all sides and angles match up cell for cell and line for line, they are congruent.
The key insight is that congruence means exact equality in every dimension, not just looking similar.
cards.misconception: A poor answer would provide two shapes with the same side lengths rearranged, which would actually make them congruent, failing to understand that different shapes can share a perimeter without being congruent.
remember: What condition must two geometric figures satisfy to be called "congruent".

cards.title: Congruence of triangles means that two triangles have the exact same shape and…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Congruence of triangles means that two triangles have the exact same shape and size, such that when one is placed over the other, they coincide completely. The corresponding sides and corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal in measurement, denoted symbolically by the symbol.
steps: Imagine you and your friend buy two identical plastic triangular set-squares from the school stationery shop in Delhi.
If you place your set-square directly on top of your friend's set-square, every edge and every corner fits over the other without any overhang.
In geometry, we call such overlapping figures congruent geometric twins.
To study them mathematically, we must match the corners (vertices) in the correct order so that side matches side and angle matches angle.
We build upon our Class 6 knowledge of basic triangle classification and shapes to understand that rigid movement—sliding, turning, or flipping—does not change a triangle's size or shape.
The key insight is that the order of letters in a triangle name matters: if ABC DEF, then vertex A matches D, B matches E, and C matches F.
cards.misconception: A poor answer merely states "they look the same" without providing a systematic method for checking corresponding vertices and measurements.
remember: If PQR XYZ, which side corresponds to side QR? A) XY B) YZ C) XZ D) YX.

cards.title: The angles opposite to the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are also equal…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The angles opposite to the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are also equal in measure, and conversely, sides opposite to equal angles are equal. This fundamental property allows us to find unknown interior angles of a triangle when only two sides or two angles are known.
steps: Imagine you are helping a carpenter in Jaipur cut triangular wooden pieces for a decorative window frame, and two of the wooden sides are measured to be exactly equal in length.
How can the carpenter be sure that the corners where these equal sides meet the base are also identical?
To begin solving this, we recall from Class 6 geometry that a triangle has three interior angles adding up to 180°, and an isosceles triangle specifically has two sides of equal length.
When two sides are equal, their 'opposite' angles—the angles facing those sides—are mirrored in value.
By identifying the equal sides first, we instantly know which two angles are equal, reducing our unknown values to a simple algebraic equation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like saying ∠ P is equal to ∠ Q shows a confusion between the vertex angle (between the equal sides) and the base angles opposite to the equal sides.
remember: In an isosceles triangle PQR, side PQ = PR. Which two angles must be equal in measure.
A student claims that if an isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°, its two base angles must each be….

cards.title: An equilateral triangle is a triangle in which all three sides are equal in…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An equilateral triangle is a triangle in which all three sides are equal in length, and consequently, all three interior angles are equal to exactly 60° each.
steps: Imagine you are helping your school craft club build a decorative star pattern using wooden triangular tiles, where every tile has sides of equal length.
If you pick up one of these tiles, you might wonder how its interior corners relate to one another without using a protractor.
In Class 6, you learned that the sum of angles in any triangle is 180° and that triangles can be classified by their sides and angles.
Building on that foundation, we now explore what happens when all three sides are equal—meaning all three angles must also be equal because equal sides subtend equal angles.
Therefore, if we divide the total sum of 180° equally among three identical angles, each angle must measure 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
This powerful property allows us to instantly identify missing angles in any equilateral triangle structure.
remember: What is the exact measure of each interior angle in an equilateral triangle.
Why must all three angles of an equilateral triangle be equal to each other.

cards.title: Two triangles are congruent by the Side-Side-Side (SSS) congruence criterion if…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Two triangles are congruent by the Side-Side-Side (SSS) congruence criterion if all three sides of one triangle are respectively equal to the three corresponding sides of another triangle. When this condition is met, the two triangles have identical shapes and sizes, meaning their corresponding angles are also equal.
steps: Imagine you and your friend are building wooden triangular roof trusses for a model house in your craft class.
You both cut three wooden sticks of lengths 5 cm, 7 cm, and 10 cm, and nail them together at their endpoints to form a triangle.

Even if your friend pushes or flips their triangle around on the desk, will it look identical to yours, or could they have built a completely different triangle using those exact same three side lengths?
To answer this, we recall from Class 6 geometry that line segments of fixed lengths can only form one unique triangle shape because the sides lock the vertices rigidly in place.

Today, we formalize this geometric rigidity into the SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence criterion, which allows us to prove two triangles are identical twins simply by measuring their three pairs of matching sides.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer—such as guessing SAS or AAA—reveals that the student is confusing side conditions with angle conditions or has not learned to check which specific parts of the triangles are given as equal.

cards.title: The SAS (Side-Angle-Side) Congruence Criterion states that two triangles are…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The SAS (Side-Angle-Side) Congruence Criterion states that two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal respectively to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle. The "included angle" is the exact angle formed between the two given sides.
steps: Imagine you are crafting two triangular wooden garden beds for your school project in New Delhi.
To ensure both garden beds are exact carbon copies (congruent) so that they fit identical metal frames, your carpenter asks you for measurements.
Instead of measuring all three sides and three angles, you realize you only need to measure two wooden planks and the exact corner angle where they meet.
When you bring those exact measurements back, the carpenter knows for sure the triangle is unique and will match every time.
To begin working with SAS, always draw a quick rough sketch of both triangles and highlight the two known sides and the angle sandwiched right between them.
We will build on our knowledge of basic line segments, angles, and general congruence from Class 6 and early Chapter 9.
cards.misconception: a wrong answer reveals: If a student chooses ∠ A or ∠ C, it shows they do not understand what "included" means. They confuse any vertex with the specific vertex where the two given sides (AB and BC) meet and share a common endpoint.

cards.title: The ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) Congruence Criterion states that if two angles and…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) Congruence Criterion states that if two angles and the included side of one triangle are equal to two angles and the included side of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. The "included side" refers to the specific side that lies directly between the two given vertices containing those angles.
steps: Imagine you are a surveyor mapping a triangular plot of land in your village schoolyard, and you need to build an identical structure on the other side of the campus without measuring all three sides.
You know the length of the brick path (the side) and the exact corner angles where it meets two fences.
How can you be sure another plot built with the same path length and corner angles will match perfectly?
Previously, you learned how to construct triangles using side-side-side and side-angle-side measurements in Class 6.
Now, we expand this to triangles defined by two angles and their connecting side.
The key insight is that fixing two angles and the length of the side between them locks the remaining triangle shape completely into place.
cards.misconception: A poor answer just states numbers without a real-world context or geometric justification.
remember: In PQR, which side is the included side between ∠ P and ∠ Q.

cards.title: The RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side) congruence criterion states that if in…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side) congruence criterion states that if in two right-angled triangles, the length of the hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are equal to the length of the hypotenuse and one corresponding side of the other triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. This specific criterion applies exclusively to right triangles because the right angle provides a fixed structural reference point.
steps: Imagine you are a carpenter in your local village building two identical triangular wooden roof supports for a storage shed.
Both supports must have a straight vertical pillar making a 90° angle with the floor, meaning they are right-angled triangles.

To make sure they are exact architectural twins without measuring every single angle, you only need to check two things: the longest slanted wooden beam (the hypotenuse) and one of the flat supporting legs.
How can measuring just these two lengths guarantee that the entire wooden structure is identical?
To begin, sketch both right-angled triangles and mark the 90° angle symbol at the vertex.
Recall from prior work that the side opposite the right angle is always the hypotenuse—the longest side of a right triangle.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "base" or "perpendicular" shows confusion regarding triangle terminology, failing to recognize that the side opposite the right angle in any right-angled triangle is always uniquely designated as the hypotenuse.
remember: In ABC, ∠ B = 90°. What is the name of the side opposite to ∠ B.
Rahul claims that if two right triangles have equal hypotenuse lengths, they must be congruent by the RHS criterion. Is Rahul correct, and why or why not.

cards.title: Applying congruence involves using known triangle congruence criteria
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Applying congruence involves using known triangle congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and corresponding parts of congruent triangles (CPCTC) to prove geometric properties, find unknown side lengths, or determine missing angle measures in complex figures.
steps: Imagine you are a builder at a construction site in Jaipur and you need to verify if two triangular support beams for a roof are exact twins so that one can replace the other.
You know their side lengths, but you need to prove whether they match completely before cutting expensive wood.
To do this, you start by writing down the given information like side lengths and angles marked on your blueprint diagram.
You connect this to what you learned about SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS criteria for triangle congruence.

The key insight is that once two triangles are proven congruent, every single corresponding side and angle must be equal—a principle known as CPCTC (Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent)—allowing you…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "nothing, because SAS only deals with two sides and an angle" reveals a misunderstanding that congruence of triangles guarantees the equality of all corresponding sides and angles, not just the ones used in the test criterion.
remember: If two triangles ABC and PQR are congruent by the SAS criterion, what does CPCTC allow us to conclude about side BC and side QR.
A student looks at two triangles and says, "They have all three pairs of sides equal, so triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $QRP$." Is the vertex matching order important….

cards.title: The Angle-Angle-Angle (AAA) condition is a set of three equal angles between…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Angle-Angle-Angle (AAA) condition is a set of three equal angles between two triangles, but it is NOT a congruence criterion because it guarantees identical shape (similarity) rather than identical size (congruence). Two triangles can have their corresponding angles exactly equal while having completely different side lengths and areas.
steps: Imagine you are drawing blueprints for a school playground slide; your little brother draws the exact same slide shape on a tiny postcard, and both drawings have identical corner angles.
If you cut out your brother's postcard drawing and try to paste it over your full-size blueprint, will they match piece-for-piece?

To begin investigating this, draw a small equilateral triangle with angles of 60°, 60°, and 60° and side lengths of 3 cm, then draw a larger equilateral triangle with the same angles but side lengths of 6 cm. Recall…
The key insight is that AAA guarantees the same shape (scaling up or down), but congruence requires at least one side length to anchor the exact physical scale.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer often claims that equal angles force triangles to be congruent, which ignores the fact that scaling a triangle up or down changes its side lengths while keeping its angles identical.
remember: What condition describes two triangles whose corresponding angles are all equal, and why is this distinct from congruence.
If Triangle PQR has angles 50°, 60°, and 70°, and Triangle XYZ also has angles 50°, 60°, and 70°, can you conclude that Triangle PQR is congruent to Triangle….
Triangle A has side lengths 4 cm, 5 cm, and 6 cm with angles 40°, 60°, and….

cards.title: Integers are a set of numbers that include all whole numbers and their negative…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Integers are a set of numbers that include all whole numbers and their negative counterparts, represented as {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3,...}, where positive integers lie to the right of zero, negative integers lie to the left of zero, and zero is neither positive nor negative.
steps: Imagine you are standing at ground level in a multi-story parking building in Delhi.
Ground level is marked as 0.
If you go up 3 floors to park your car, we call that $+3$ (positive 3).
If you take the elevator down 2 floors to the basement to check the electricity meter, we call that $-2$ (negative 2).
To understand integers fully, we expand our whole numbers by introducing a mirror image of counting numbers to the left of zero.
We write positive numbers with a plus sign (or no sign) and negative numbers with a minus sign.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer that picks Shimla because 4 is less than 7 shows the student is comparing the digits while ignoring the negative signs, which reverse the order of magnitude on the number line.
remember: Which of the following numbers is considered neither a positive integer nor a negative integer? A) $+1$ B) $0$ C) $-1$ D) Both A and C.
Shimla records -4 degree Celsius and Srinagar records -7 degree Celsius. Which place is colder, and by what number-line reasoning.
An elevator starts at the ground floor ($0$).….

cards.title: The addition of integers using a number line is a visual method where positive…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The addition of integers using a number line is a visual method where positive integers are added by moving to the right and negative integers are added by moving to the left from a starting number. This process physically models how positive and negative values combine on a linear scale.
steps: Imagine you are playing a board game where your score is currently at $-3$ (3 points in debt), and you roll a dice that gives you $+5$ points.
Where does your final score land on the scoring track?
To solve this, we start at our initial position on the number line and use directional movement: positive numbers mean moving right (forward), and negative numbers mean moving left (backward).
This builds directly on comparing and ordering integers from Class 6, where you learned to locate positive and negative numbers on a number line.
The key insight is that the operation of addition combined with a negative integer translates physically to a leftward step, exactly opposite to adding a positive integer.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer—such as saying "to the left"—reveals a confusion between positive and negative directions, often mixing up the rules of addition with subtraction or treating all numbers as positive.
remember: What direction on a horizontal number line do you move when adding a positive integer.
Explain why adding a negative integer, such as $-4$, requires moving to the left on the number line instead of the right.
Use a number line method to find the sum: $(-3) + (+5)$.

cards.title: Subtraction of integers involves finding the difference between two integers by…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Subtraction of integers involves finding the difference between two integers by adding the additive inverse of the subtrahend to the minuend, following the algebraic rule $a - b = a + (-b)$ and $a - (-b) = a + b$.
steps: Imagine you are checking the weather report in Srinagar, where the morning temperature is -3^ and it drops by 5^ by night.
How do we calculate the final temperature using subtraction of integers?
We begin by writing down the starting integer and the subtraction operation, just like we did with whole numbers in earlier grades.
However, when subtracting a positive or a negative integer, we must remember our prior learning about additive inverses and number lines.
The key insight is turning a subtraction problem into an addition problem by changing the sign of the subtrahend: subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite.
cards.misconception: A poor answer uses only whole numbers or ignores the integer rules, revealing a lack of comprehension regarding negative values.
remember: What is the result of evaluating the expression $-7 - (-4)$.
Explain why subtracting a positive integer, such as $8 - 12$, moves us to the left on the number line, whereas subtracting a negative integer, such as $8 - (-12)$, moves us to the….
Calculate the value of $-15 - 8 - (-25)$ step by step.

cards.title: The sign rules for multiplication of integers state that the product of two…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The sign rules for multiplication of integers state that the product of two integers with like signs (both positive or both negative) is always a positive integer, while the product of two integers with unlike signs (one positive and one negative) is always a negative integer.
steps: Imagine you are managing a school canteen bank account where a fee deduction of 5 rupees per day is recorded as -5.
If this deduction happens for 4 consecutive days, what is the total change in your account balance?
To solve this, we need to multiply a negative integer by a positive integer, building upon our understanding of repeated addition of integers from Class 6.
We write down the repeated addition as (-5) + (-5) + (-5) + (-5) = -20, which corresponds to the multiplication expression 4 × (-5).

The key insight is that multiplication is repeated addition, and extending this to negative numbers gives us the fundamental sign rules: positive times negative is negative, and negative times negative is positive.
cards.misconception: A poor answer uses incorrect signs, resulting in a positive product instead of a negative one.
remember: What is the product of $-7$ and $8$.
Explain why multiplying $-4$ by $-3$ results in a positive $12$ rather than a negative $12$.
Calculate the value of (-12) × (-5) × 3.

cards.title: The multiplication of two negative integers always yields a positive product…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The multiplication of two negative integers always yields a positive product because multiplying opposite directions on a number line twice reverses the orientation back to the positive side. Formally, for any positive integers a and b, (-a) × (-b) = +(a × b).
steps: Imagine you are playing a video game where walking backwards (negative direction) away from a trap is rewarded, but your scorekeeper reverses your penalties twice!
When you multiply two negative quantities, think of it as reversing a debt twice, which turns it into a credit.
We start by reviewing Class 6 multiplication of positive and negative numbers.
Then, we look at the pattern of products as multipliers decrease: (-3) × 3 = -9, (-3) × 2 = -6, (-3) × 1 = -3, (-3) × 0 = 0, following this pattern, (-3) × (-1) must be +3.
The key rule is: negative times negative equals positive.
remember: What is the sign of the product when you multiply two negative integers together.
Explain why (-5) × (-4) results in a positive number rather than a negative number using a pattern approach.
Calculate the exact value of (-12) × (-7).

cards.title: The product of a positive integer and a negative integer is always a negative…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The product of a positive integer and a negative integer is always a negative integer, found by multiplying their absolute values and attaching a negative sign. For any two positive whole numbers a and b, (-a) × b = -(a × b) and a × (-b) = -(a × b).
steps: Imagine you borrow 5 rupees from your friend every day for 4 days in a row, meaning your account change each day is -5 rupees.
To find your total balance change after 4 days, you need to calculate 4 × (-5), which means adding -5 four times: (-5) + (-5) + (-5) + (-5) = -20.
To begin solving these without writing out long addition chains, we write down the numbers and multiply their absolute values first, just like whole numbers.
Then, we apply the core rule: multiplying numbers with unlike signs always results in a negative product.
Connecting this back to our number line and whole number multiplication from Class 6, we see that scaling in the negative direction flips the sign of the product.
The key insight is that a positive multiplier tells us how many groups we have, while the negative integer tells us the size and direction of each group.
cards.misconception: A poor answer would use two positive numbers or fail to incorporate a negative integer representing a loss or downward direction.
remember: What is the product of $+7$ and $-8$.
Explain why multiplying a positive integer by a negative integer results in a negative product using the concept of repeated addition.
Calculate the value of (-12) × 6.

cards.title: The commutative property of integer multiplication states that changing the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The commutative property of integer multiplication states that changing the order of two integers being multiplied does not change their product; mathematically expressed as a × b = b × a for any integers a and b.
steps: Imagine you are at a school sports event in Delhi, arranging chairs for the annual function.
You have 5 rows of chairs, and each row has (-3) extra chairs allocated or removed due to spacing adjustments, giving you a quick calculation of 5 × (-3).
Alternatively, if you calculate (-3) rows of 5 units each, how does the product compare?
To begin, write down both expressions side by side: 5 × (-3) and (-3) × 5.
Recall from your earlier work with integer multiplication sign rules that a positive integer multiplied by a negative integer results in a negative product.
Compute each side independently to find that both equal -15.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer that calls the bracket move itself commutative shows the student confuses the property that changes grouping with the property that changes the position of factors.
remember: Which of the following mathematical statements correctly demonstrates the commutative property of multiplication for integers -8 and….
Rahul claims that (-5) × (-6) is not equal to (-6) × (-5) because the negative signs shift positions when you rewrite the….
Calculate the value of 14 × (-9) using the commutative property of multiplication by first rewriting the expression with (-9) as the first multiplier. What is the final product.

cards.title: The division of integers follows specific sign rules…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The division of integers follows specific sign rules: dividing two integers with like signs (both positive or both negative) yields a positive quotient, while dividing two integers with unlike signs (one positive and one negative) yields a negative quotient. This is expressed mathematically as (+) ÷ (+) = (+), (-)÷ (-) = (+), (+) ÷ (-) = (-), and (-)÷ (+) = (-), provided the divisor is not zero.
steps: Imagine a shopkeeper in your local market who finds that his total loss over 4 days is ₹200, and the loss was exactly the same amount every single day. To find out how much money he lost each day, you need to share or…

Just like in multiplication where two negatives make a positive, in division, the relationship between inverse operations helps us see that dividing a negative number by a positive number must result in a negative…
We first recall how to divide whole numbers (absolute values) and then apply the sign rules we learned for multiplication.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to determine the exact sign and value of any integer division problem instantly.
remember: What is the value of (-48) ÷ (-6).
A student says that because 5 × (-4) = -20, therefore (-20) ÷ 5 must be +4. Is this statement correct, and why or why not.
Calculate the quotient for the integer expression: [(-72) ÷ 9] ÷ (-2).

cards.title: Word problems with integers involve translating real-world scenarios—such as…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Word problems with integers involve translating real-world scenarios—such as changing temperatures, depths below sea level, or financial balances—into mathematical expressions using positive and negative integers, and then applying integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division to solve them. The final result must be interpreted back into the real-world context with proper units.
steps: Imagine you are standing on a balcony 15 metres above ground level, and you drop a heavy parcel down into an underground parking basement that is 5 metres below ground level.
How would you calculate the total vertical distance the parcel travels?
To solve this, we must first translate words like "above" into positive integers (+15) and "below" into negative integers (-5).
We connect this to our prior knowledge of integers on a number line and integer subtraction rules.
The key insight is that words like "rise," "gain," "above," and "deposit" represent positive integers, while "drop," "loss," "below," and "withdrawal" represent negative integers.
remember: At 6:00 PM, the temperature in Shimla was 2 °C. By midnight, the temperature dropped by 5 °C. Which integer represents the temperature at midnight.
A submarine is situated 450 metres below sea….
A miner is working in a coal mine at an elevation of -65 metres. If he climbs up a ladder to a platform that is 25 metres above his current position, what is his new elevation.

cards.title: Patterns in integer operations involve observing, analyzing…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Patterns in integer operations involve observing, analyzing, and generalizing regularities or predictable behaviors when applying arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) to positive and negative integers. By recognizing these patterns, students can discover and verify fundamental mathematical properties such as commutativity, associativity, distributivity, and sign rules without performing tedious calculations.
steps: Imagine you are helping a school canteen manager in Mumbai track their daily profit and loss over a week.
If the canteen loses 50 rupees each day (-50) for 4 consecutive days, how do we write that as a mathematical expression, and what pattern emerges if we look at losing money over fewer or more days?
To begin, we write out a sequence of calculations: (-50) × 3 = -150, (-50) × 2 = -100, (-50) × 1 = -50, and (-50) × 0 = 0.
Connecting this to our prior knowledge of multiplication and number lines, we notice that as the multiplier decreases by 1, the product increases by 50.
The key insight is that patterns allow us to predict unknown products and quotients, such as (-50) × (-1) = +50, by extending the established rule of the sequence.
cards.misconception: A poor answer shows random numbers without following the systematic decrease of the divisor or fails to show how division by negative numbers yields positive quotients.
remember: Why does the product of two negative integers, such as (-4) × (-3), always result in a positive integer (+12) when analyzed through a decreasing multiplier pattern.
Complete the missing steps and find the final value of the pattern: $15 - 3 = 12$, $15 - 6 = 9$, $15 - 9 = 6$, $15 - 12 =….

cards.title: Common factors of two numbers are the whole numbers that divide both given…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Common factors of two numbers are the whole numbers that divide both given numbers exactly without leaving any remainder. In other words, they are the intersection of the factor sets of both numbers.
steps: Imagine you are organizing a school sports event and have 12 red flags and 18 blue flags.
You want to divide both types of flags into identical rows so that no flags are left over, asking: what are the possible sizes of equal groups we can make?
To solve this, we begin by listing every single factor of 12 and every single factor of 18 using our knowledge of multiplication tables.
Building on our Class 6 work with factors and multiples, we find numbers that divide both 12 and 18.
The key insight is that the numbers appearing in both lists are our common factors.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "a number that is added to both" shows confusion between factors and addition, or confusing factors with multiples.
remember: What is the definition of a common factor of two numbers.
Why is the number 1 always a common factor for any two positive whole numbers? Explain briefly.
Find all the common factors of the numbers 24 and 36.

cards.title: The Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two or more numbers is the greatest positive…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two or more numbers is the greatest positive integer that divides each of those numbers completely without leaving any remainder. It represents the ultimate sharing capacity or the largest uniform grouping possible for given quantities.
steps: Imagine you are organizing a school cultural fest in Delhi and have 24 red ribbons and 36 blue ribbons.
You want to make identical gift hampers such that every hamper has the exact same number of red ribbons and the exact same number of blue ribbons, with none left over.
To find the maximum number of identical hampers you can make, you need to find the factors that are shared by both 24 and 36.
You learned about factors and divisibility rules in Class 6, where you found individual factors like $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24$ for 24.
Now, by comparing the factor lists of both numbers, we locate all numbers that divide both, called common factors.
The largest of these common factors is our Highest Common Factor, which tells us the exact maximum number of identical gift hampers we can create.
cards.misconception: A poor answer would use numbers whose HCF is not 6 or use prime numbers instead of composite numbers.
remember: What does HCF stand for, and what does it mathematically signify when comparing two numbers like 12 and 18.
Rahul says that the HCF of two numbers can sometimes be larger than both of the numbers themselves. Is Rahul correct? Explain why or why not.
Find all the common factors of 30 and 45, and state their HCF.

cards.title: Finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) by the listing factors method involves…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) by the listing factors method involves writing down all the individual factors of two or more given numbers, identifying which factors appear on all the lists (common factors), and selecting the largest one among them. This method directly translates the foundational concept of factors into finding the greatest shared divisor for quantities like grouping items or simplifying ratios.
steps: Imagine you are organizing a school cultural event at your school in Delhi, and you have 24 red ribbons and 36 blue ribbons.
You want to cut them into identical pieces of maximum possible length without any ribbons left over so that each stage decoration looks uniform.
To figure out the maximum possible length, you need to find the factors of 24 and the factors of 36.
We begin by recalling what a factor is: a whole number that divides another number completely without leaving a remainder.
By writing down every single factor for both numbers in systematic pairs, we can spot which factors are shared by both.
Finally, we look at those shared factors and pick the highest one, which gives us our maximum ribbon length.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer usually reveals that the student is confusing factors with multiples, such as thinking factors are numbers obtained by multiplying by 2, 3, etc., rather than numbers that divide evenly into the given number.
remember: What is the exact definition of a "factor" of a number when listing factors to find an HCF.
When listing factors of 18, a student writes: $1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18$. Are all these numbers factors, and how do we know we haven't missed any.
Find the HCF of 24 and 30 by listing all their factors. Show the common factors and state the highest one.

cards.title: The Prime Factorisation Method for finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Prime Factorisation Method for finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) involves expressing each given number as a product of its prime factors, and then finding the product of the lowest powers of all common prime factors. This method breaks down large numbers into their fundamental building blocks to efficiently find the greatest common divisor without listing all individual factors.
steps: Imagine you are organizing a school cultural festival and have 72 red ribbons and 90 blue ribbons.
You want to cut them into pieces of equal length without any ribbons left over, and you want each piece to be as long as possible.
To figure out the maximum possible length, you need to find the highest common factor of 72 and 90.
Listing every single factor manually for large numbers is time-consuming and prone to missing factors.
Instead, we can build on what you learned in Class 6 about factor trees and divisibility rules to break each number down into pure prime numbers.

The key insight is that any number's hidden structure is revealed through its prime factorisation, and the HCF is simply built from the shared prime building blocks raised to their lowest common powers.
cards.misconception: A poor answer would choose numbers outside the range or numbers whose prime factorisation does not yield an HCF of 14 (e.g., sharing other common factors that inflate the HCF).
remember: What is the prime factorisation of the number 72 expressed in exponential form.
When finding the HCF of two numbers using prime factorisation, why do we select the lowest power of the common prime factors rather than the highest power.
Find the HCF of 54 and 72 using the prime factorisation method. Show your prime factorisation steps clearly.

cards.title: The Euclidean Division Method for finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) is an…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Euclidean Division Method for finding the Highest Common Factor (HCF) is an efficient step-by-step procedure based on repeated division, where the last non-zero remainder represents the HCF of two numbers.
steps: Imagine you are a school event coordinator dividing 156 long wooden desks and 96 plastic chairs into exact, identical rows for an assembly, leaving no leftovers of either type.
Instead of listing every single factor or drawing massive prime factor trees, mathematicians use a clever shortcut called the Euclidean Division Method.
To begin, you divide the larger number by the smaller number, just like you learned in earlier division operations, and note down the remainder.
Then, you take the previous divisor, make it your new dividend, take the remainder as your new divisor, and repeat this cycle.

The key insight is that the common factors of two numbers do not change if you replace the larger number by its remainder when divided by the smaller number, making even large numbers simple to handle.
cards.misconception: A poor answer lists random numbers without checking the exact number of steps required.
remember: What is the mathematical term for the number that is left over when you divide one integer by another during the Euclidean division process.
Why does the Euclidean Division Method require us to replace the original dividend with the previous divisor, and the previous divisor with the remainder, in each successive step.
Use the Euclidean Division Method to find the HCF of 135 and 225. Show the division steps clearly.

cards.title: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two or more non-zero whole numbers is the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two or more non-zero whole numbers is the smallest positive whole number that is a multiple of each of the given numbers. It represents the first point in time or value where the individual patterns or cycles of the given numbers align completely.
steps: Imagine two friends running around a school running track in India.
Amit completes one round every 4 minutes, and Priya completes one round every 6 minutes.
If they start running together at the exact same moment from the starting line, when will they both cross the starting line together again?
To solve this, we can list the minutes at which Amit passes (4, 8, 12, 16, 20...) and the minutes at which Priya passes (6, 12, 18, 24...).
We look for the smallest time number that appears in both lists, which is 12 minutes!
Building on our prior knowledge of factors and multiples from Class 6, we now formalize this concept as the Least Common Multiple (LCM).
cards.misconception: A poor answer lists numbers randomly without verifying their HCF and LCM, showing a lack of structural understanding of number properties.
remember: What is the definition of the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers.
Rahul says that the LCM of 4 and 6 is 24 because 4 × 6 = 24. Is Rahul correct, and why or why not.
Find the LCM of 12 and 18 by listing their first few non-zero multiples.

cards.title: Finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) by the listing multiples method…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) by the listing multiples method involves writing out the non-zero multiples of each given number in increasing order, identifying the common multiples they share, and selecting the smallest one among those common multiples.
steps: Imagine two school bell rings: one bell rings every 6 minutes and another bell rings every 8 minutes.
If both bells ring together right now, after how many minutes will they ring together again for the first time?
To solve this, we need to track the exact minutes when each bell sounds by writing down their multiples.
Building on our knowledge of factors and multiples from Class 6, we can systematically list the table of multiples for each number.
The key insight is that the "least common multiple" is simply the smallest number that appears on every list of multiples we generate.
cards.misconception: A poor answer gives numbers whose LCM is not 12, such as 3 and 5 (LCM 15), showing a failure to work backward from a target LCM.
remember: What is the definition of the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers.
When listing multiples to find the LCM of 4 and 6, why do we stop listing once we find the first number that appears in both lists.
Find the LCM of 5 and 7 by listing their first few multiples.

cards.title: Finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) by prime factorisation involves…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) by prime factorisation involves expressing each given number as a product of its prime factors, and then taking the highest power of every prime factor present in any of the factorisations to find their product. This method is much faster for large numbers than listing all multiples.
steps: Imagine two school bell rings at a morning assembly: one bell rings every 12 seconds and another bell rings every 18 seconds.
If they both ring together right now, after how many seconds will they ring together again?
To solve this, we need to find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of 12 and 18, which tells us the earliest time their cycles align.
While listing multiples works for small numbers, it becomes too slow when numbers get larger like 120 and 210.
Instead, we break down each number into its basic building blocks using prime factorisation, just like you learned in Class 6.
By comparing the prime factors of each number, we can systematically build the smallest number that contains both of them as factors.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 2 × 3^3 reveals that the student has confused the counts of prime factors or made a multiplication error when dividing by prime numbers (e.g., 36 ÷ 2 = 18, 18 ÷ 2 = 9, 9 ÷ 3 = 3, 3 ÷ 3 = 1).
remember: What is the prime factorisation of 36 expressed in exponential form.
When finding the LCM of two numbers using prime factorisation, why do we choose the highest power of each prime factor instead of the lowest power.
Find the LCM of 24 and 36 using prime factorisation.

cards.title: The product of the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and the Least Common Multiple…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The product of the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of any two positive integers is always equal to the product of the two numbers themselves (HCF × LCM = Product of the two numbers). This fundamental property allows us to find the LCM or HCF of two numbers quickly if their product and one of the values are known.
steps: Imagine you are helping at a school stationery shop in Delhi, and you notice a curious pattern when packing notebooks and pens in bundles.
If you take two specific numbers, say 12 and 18, their HCF is 6 and their LCM is 36.
If you multiply the two numbers (12 × 18 = 216), and then multiply their HCF and LCM (6 × 36 = 216), you get the exact same result!
To begin exploring this, write down two small numbers, find their prime factorisation using division or factor trees, compute both HCF and LCM from Class 6 concepts, and then multiply them.
Connect this to your prior knowledge of prime factorisation and multiplication.
The key insight is that this relationship acts as a mathematical shortcut and a verification tool for any pair of numbers.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as "the sum of the two numbers" or "their difference" shows confusion between basic arithmetic operations and the structural properties of prime factors. Students often guess when they have not memorised or conceptualised the rule.
remember: What does the product of the HCF and LCM of two positive integers always equal.
If the product of two numbers is 300, and their HCF is 5, can their LCM be 45? Explain why or why not using the relationship between HCF and LCM.

cards.title: Applications of HCF and LCM in Real-Life Problems involve translating everyday…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Applications of HCF and LCM in Real-Life Problems involve translating everyday situations—such as scheduling events, dividing items into equal groups, or aligning periodic occurrences—into mathematical operations using the Highest Common Factor (HCF) or Least Common Multiple (LCM). HCF is used when we need to break things down into smaller, equal pieces or find the maximum possible size of groups, while LCM is used when we need to find when periodic events will happen together again or build up to a common total.
steps: Imagine you visit a school sports day where two different whistles blow: one blows every 6 seconds and the other blows every 8 seconds.
If they both just blew together, when is the exact next time they will blow at the exact same moment?
To solve this, you need to find a common multiple of both 6 and 8, specifically the smallest one, which means using the Least Common Multiple (LCM).

Conversely, if you have two ribbons of length 36 cm and 48 cm and want to cut them into equal-sized pieces of the maximum possible length without any waste, you are looking for the Highest Common Factor (HCF).

Connecting back to our foundational knowledge of factors and multiples, we translate words like "greatest," "maximum," or "divide equally" into HCF, and words like "together," "simultaneous," "next time," or "minimum…
cards.misconception: A poor answer would give numbers that don't match the required LCM calculation or describe a partitioning scenario instead of a recurring cycle.
remember: A school bell rings every 30 minutes and a bus leaves the gate every 45….

cards.title: Common multiples are numbers that are exact multiples of two or more given…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Common multiples are numbers that are exact multiples of two or more given numbers, sharing properties such as the cyclical appearance of intersection points and being exact multiples of the Least Common Multiple (LCM).
steps: Imagine you and your friend are running on a circular athletic track at your school sports ground.
You complete one full round every 4 minutes, while your friend completes one round every 6 minutes.
Both of you start running together from the starting line at minute 0.
When will both of you cross the starting line together again?
To figure this out, we write down the minutes at which you cross (4, 8, 12, 16, 20...) and the minutes at which your friend crosses (6, 12, 18, 24...).
We look for numbers that appear in both lists—these are our common multiples!
cards.misconception: A poor answer fails to use the LCM or miscalculates the multiple step.

cards.title: Decimals are an extension of our place value system used to represent numbers…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Decimals are an extension of our place value system used to represent numbers smaller than one by utilizing powers of ten in the denominator, separated from the whole number part by a decimal point. Each position to the right of the decimal point represents a fractional value divided by 10, 100, 1,000, and so on.
steps: Imagine you are at a vegetable market in India buying 2 kilograms and 350 grams of potatoes, and the shopkeeper writes the price tag as ₹45.75.
How do we understand what the.75 actually means in terms of parts of a whole?
We begin by recalling that our place value system grows larger by multiplying by 10 as we move left, so it must shrink by dividing by 10 as we move right past the ones place.
Connect this to fractions, where tenths ((1)/(10)) and hundredths ((1)/(100)) are just another way of writing parts of a whole.

The key insight is that the decimal point is a fixed anchor: digits to the left are whole numbers (ones, tens, hundreds), while digits to the right are fractional parts (tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
cards.misconception: A poor answer fails one or more constraints, such as ignoring the place value ratio or miscalculating the digit sum, revealing a weak grasp of multi-constraint number composition.
remember: What is the place value of the digit $7$ in the decimal number $45.278$.

cards.title: Multiplying a decimal number by a whole number involves multiplying the numbers…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multiplying a decimal number by a whole number involves multiplying the numbers as if they were whole numbers, and then placing the decimal point in the product so that it has the same number of decimal places as the original decimal factor.
steps: Imagine you are buying 4 notebooks for school, and each notebook costs ₹24.75.
To find the total cost, you need to calculate 4 × 24.75, which means adding 24.75 four times.
Just as you learned to multiply large numbers and handle fractions in earlier classes, we can look at decimals as fractions with denominators of 10, 100, or 1000.
To begin without getting confused by the dot, write down the numbers and multiply them as if they were standard whole numbers.
Finally, count how many digits are behind the decimal point in your decimal factor, and place the decimal point in your answer from right to left so it has the exact same count.
The key insight is that multiplying a decimal by a whole number scales the decimal value just like scaling a fraction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "always put the decimal point after two digits" reveals a rigid memorization of money problems rather than understanding place value, while "align the decimal points as in addition" shows confusion between addition/subtraction rules and…

cards.title: Multiplying two decimal numbers involves multiplying their whole number values…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Multiplying two decimal numbers involves multiplying their whole number values as if no decimal points exist, and then placing the decimal point in the product so that the total number of decimal places equals the sum of the decimal places in both multipliers.
steps: Imagine you go to a local stationery shop in India and buy 2.5 kg of handmade chart paper, and the cost of the paper is ₹15.50 per kilogram.
To find out the total amount you need to pay, you must multiply 15.50 by 2.5.
Just like you learned how to multiply fractions and whole numbers, you can start by ignoring the decimal points temporarily and treating the numbers as whole integers (1550 and 25).

After finding their whole number product, you count how many total digits are to the right of the decimal points in both original numbers (two digits in 15.50 and one digit in 2.5, making a total of three decimal…
The key insight is that the product's decimal point must be moved three places from right to left, turning the whole number product into the correct decimal currency value.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as aligning the decimal points vertically (like in addition) reveals a confusion between addition/subtraction rules and multiplication rules of decimals.
remember: What is the rule for determining the position of the decimal point when multiplying two decimal numbers like 0.4 × 0.05.

cards.title: Decimal division by a whole number is the process of splitting a decimal…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Decimal division by a whole number is the process of splitting a decimal quantity into a specified number of equal whole parts, achieved by dividing the whole number part first and then placing the decimal point in the quotient directly above the dividend's decimal point before dividing the decimal parts.
steps: Imagine you and 4 friends pool your money and find you have saved a total of ₹48.75 to buy shared craft supplies, and you need to split the cost equally among all 5 of you. How much does each person pay?
To solve this, you begin by setting up long division just like you would with whole numbers, writing the dividend 48.75 inside the division bracket and the whole number divisor 5 outside.
You recall from Class 6 place value that decimals are just extensions of our place value system, where tenths and hundredths follow the exact same grouping rules as tens and ones.

The key insight is that when your long division reaches the decimal point in the dividend, you immediately place a decimal point directly above in your quotient row, and then continue dividing standard place values…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "move the decimal point to the right based on the number of zeros" reveals confusion between multiplying/dividing by powers of 10 and standard long division by a general whole…
remember: What is the rule for placing the decimal point in the quotient when dividing a decimal number by a whole number using long division.
Explain why 12.6 ÷ 3 yields 4.2 instead of 42 or 0.42. How does place value ensure the decimal point stays in the correct position.

cards.title: Dividing a decimal number by another decimal number involves converting the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Dividing a decimal number by another decimal number involves converting the divisor into a whole number by multiplying both the dividend and the divisor by the same power of 10 ($10, 100, 1000$, etc.), and then performing whole-number division to find the quotient.
steps: Imagine you bought 2.5 kilograms of sweet jalebis for a school celebration, and you want to pack them into small paper cones, each holding 0.5 kilograms.
How many cones can you fill?
To find out, you need to divide 2.5 by 0.5, which means dividing a decimal by a decimal.
Just like we learned when we studied fractions as division, dividing by a decimal is tricky because the divisor has a fractional part.
To make it easy, we use equivalent fractions or shifting decimal points: we multiply both numbers by 10 so the divisor becomes a whole number.
Then, the problem becomes 25 ÷ 5, which is much easier to solve!
cards.misconception: A wrong answer usually shows that the student only shifted the decimal point in the dividend or tried to ignore the decimal point in the divisor entirely, which changes the value of the expression.
