cards.title: A real image is formed when light rays actually intersect after reflection or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A real image is formed when light rays actually intersect after reflection or refraction, and it can be caught on a screen. A virtual image is formed when light rays appear to diverge from a point behind a reflecting or refracting surface, and it cannot be caught on a screen.

Recall from your earlier studies that light travels in straight lines and bounces off mirrors.
Today, we will explore why some images can be touched and projected onto a screen while others exist only as an optical illusion to our eyes.

cards.title: The rotation of the Earth is the spinning of the Earth on its imaginary axis…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The rotation of the Earth is the spinning of the Earth on its imaginary axis from west to east, completing one full rotation in approximately 24 hours, which causes the cycle of day and night. The physical quantity measured here is time period (hours, seconds) and angular displacement (degrees, radians), with the SI unit for time being the second (s).
steps: Observe how a ceiling fan spins around a fixed central metal rod in your classroom.

If you stick a small glowing torch light on one wall and rotate a globe or a ball in front of it, you will notice that only one half of the ball gets illuminated by the torch light while the other half remains in shadow.
As you slowly spin the ball, the side that was in darkness rotates into the light, and the side that was in light moves into darkness.
This simple observation mirrors how the Earth rotates on its axis relative to the Sun. We measure this motion by tracking the passage of time over a 24-hour day-night cycle.

Connecting back to our prior understanding of how light travels in straight lines and forms shadows, the Sun acts as the light source, and the opaque Earth blocks light to cast a massive shadow on its night-facing side.

cards.title: The apparent movement of the Sun across the sky refers to the daily…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The apparent movement of the Sun across the sky refers to the daily east-to-west motion of the Sun from our perspective on Earth, caused by the Earth's actual rotation from west to east on its axis. While measured quantitatively in degrees per hour (°/h) of angular displacement, it is fundamentally a geometric perspective of celestial motion.
steps: Stand in your courtyard or look out a west-facing window in the morning and notice where sunlight enters your room; by afternoon, notice how the patch of light has shifted completely across the floor.

To understand this, remember how objects appear to rush backward when you look out the window of a moving train or school bus. Similarly, as our home planet rotates eastward on its axis, our viewpoint constantly shifts…

cards.title: The revolution of the Earth is the movement of the Earth in a nearly circular…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The revolution of the Earth is the movement of the Earth in a nearly circular or elliptical orbit around the Sun, completing one full circuit in approximately 365.25 days (one year). This orbital motion, combined with Earth's axial tilt, is measured in time units such as days and years, and is responsible for the changing seasons.

steps: When you look at the night sky from your school rooftop in Diwali compared to when you are on summer vacation, you notice completely different star patterns like Orion or the Big Dipper.
To understand why this happens, recall how Earth moves in an orbit around the Sun over a full year.
As Earth travels along this orbital path, the dark night-side of our planet faces a different direction of deep space every few months.
Connecting this yearly orbital motion to the changing background stars explains why certain constellations disappear and reappear seasonally.

cards.title: Seasons on Earth are repeating periods of the year characterized by distinct…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Seasons on Earth are repeating periods of the year characterized by distinct patterns of weather and daylight hours, caused by the combination of Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt and its revolution around the Sun. The physical quantity measured is solar energy flux (insolation) per unit area in watts per square meter (W/m^2).

When you tilt a flashlight beam directly onto a table, the light patch is small, bright, and concentrated, but when you tilt the table or the light, the patch spreads out and becomes dimmer.
Connect this to how Earth orbits the Sun while tilted at an angle of 23.5 degrees.
Throughout this journey, different hemispheres tilt toward or away from the Sun, changing both the angle of sunlight and the length of daylight.
The key physical principle is that concentrated rays spread over a smaller area deliver higher thermal energy per square meter.

cards.title: An eclipse occurs when one celestial body moves into the shadow of another…

By analyzing the tilt of the Moon's orbit, we discover that eclipses happen only during specific alignment seasons when the new or full moon matches these intersection points.

cards.title: A solar eclipse is an astronomical phenomenon that occurs when the Moon passes…

cards.definition: A solar eclipse is an astronomical phenomenon that occurs when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, casting a shadow on Earth's surface and temporarily blocking all or part of the Sun's light. It is measured by the alignment geometry and duration (in minutes and seconds) along specific geographic paths.
steps: Imagine standing outside on a sunny afternoon in your school courtyard when suddenly a large playground ball is held close to your eye, completely blocking your view of a distant street lamp.
In space, a similar alignment happens when the Moon orbits Earth and moves directly along the straight line connecting the Sun and Earth.

cards.title: A lunar eclipse is an astronomical event that occurs when the Earth passes…

steps: Imagine standing outside on a clear night with a streetlamp behind you, holding your hand out so that your hand casts a shadow on a wall.
A lunar eclipse works on the exact same principle of shadow formation that you learned about with light in Class 6, but on a cosmic scale!
Instead of a streetlamp, we have the Sun; instead of your body, we have the massive Earth blocking light; and instead of a wall, we have the Moon passing through Earth's shadow.

As the Moon revolves around the Earth, the half facing the Sun is always lit, but our viewpoint from Earth changes.
By tracking how much of that lit half we can see each night, we map out the lunar cycle.

cards.title: The Earth's axis is an imaginary straight line passing through its North and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Earth's axis is an imaginary straight line passing through its North and South poles, tilted at an angle of 23.5° away from the perpendicular to its orbital plane (or 66.5° to the orbital plane). This fixed tilt, measured in degrees (°), is permanent and determines how solar radiation is distributed across the planet's surface throughout the year.
steps: Imagine spinning a playground top or a globe on your desk—notice how it spins around a central rod or line without wobbling off center.

If you tilt that globe slightly while moving it in a circle around a desk lamp representing the Sun, you will see that different parts of the globe receive direct light at different points in the circle.
Building on your knowledge of how Earth revolves around the Sun in an orbit, we introduce the concept that Earth does not stand straight up and down relative to its path.
Instead, its rotation axis is permanently tilted at an angle of 23.5°.
This specific angle and the constant parallel orientation of the axis as Earth orbits are the fundamental reasons behind the changing seasons and varying day lengths we experience.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as 90° or 0° reveals a failure to recall the specific geometric measurement of Earth's tilt, confusing it with a completely upright or completely flat orientation.

cards.title: Acids and bases are two major classes of chemical substances defined by their…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Acids and bases are two major classes of chemical substances defined by their distinct properties, where acids generally taste sour and turn blue litmus red, while bases taste bitter, feel soapy to the touch, and turn red litmus blue, with properties measured through chemical reactivity and pH indicators.

cards.title: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens used as an indicator to test…

steps: Imagine adding a spoonful of yellow turmeric powder to a white cotton shirt while eating dal, and when your mother washes it with soap, the yellow stain suddenly turns reddish-brown!
To understand why this happens, we begin by observing how colored plant parts react when mixed with everyday household substances like lemon juice or soap water.

cards.title: A neutral substance is a chemical substance that is neither acidic nor basic…

cards.definition: A neutral substance is a chemical substance that is neither acidic nor basic, having a balanced concentration of hydrogen and hydroxide ions that results in no color change when tested with universal indicators. Recall that acids turn blue litmus red and bases turn red litmus blue; neutral substances are those that leave indicator colors completely unaffected.
By recording these observations systematically, we classify substances that show no color shift in both red and blue litmus as neutral.
This leads us to understand that neutrality is a middle state of chemical behavior, where neither acidic nor basic properties dominate.

cards.definition: A neutralisation reaction is a chemical process in which an acid reacts completely with a base to produce a salt and water, releasing heat in the process. While chemistry measures this in moles and concentration, its physical manifestation involves temperature change and the formation of a neutral product with no excess hydrogen or hydroxide ions.
steps: When you touch a test tube in the school laboratory in which dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are mixed, you notice the glass feels remarkably warm to the touch.
This warmth tells us that energy is being released, connecting back to our prior studies of heat flow and thermal energy changes in chemical processes.
To understand this, we measure the temperature before and after mixing equal strengths of acidic and basic solutions.
We find that the resulting mixture is neither acidic nor basic—it is neutral, changing litmus paper to neither red nor blue.
The fundamental principle governing this is the conservation of matter and energy, expressed through the word equation: Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat.

cards.title: The pH scale is a numerical scale ranging from 0 to 14 used to specify how…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The pH scale is a numerical scale ranging from 0 to 14 used to specify how acidic or basic (alkaline) an aqueous solution is, measured in dimensionless units. A pH value of 7 is neutral, values less than 7 indicate acidity (with lower values representing stronger acids), and values greater than 7 indicate basicity (with higher values representing stronger bases).
steps: When testing tap water or lemon juice with natural indicators like litmus or turmeric, you notice a color change, but simple indicators only tell you if a substance is an acid or a base, not how strong it is. To measure…
Think of it like a thermometer, but instead of measuring temperature in degrees Celsius, it measures the concentration of hydrogen ions using numbers from 0 to 14.
We begin by observing the color produced when a universal indicator paper is dipped into a solution and matching that color to a standard reference chart.
Building on our prior knowledge of natural and synthetic indicators, the pH scale provides a standardized global tool for precise measurement.
The key principle is: pH < 7 is acidic, pH = 7 is neutral, and pH > 7 is basic.

cards.title: Acids and bases play a crucial role in our everyday lives…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Acids and bases play a crucial role in our everyday lives, determining the chemical nature of substances we consume, use for cleaning, and encounter in nature. They are measured qualitatively through their chemical behavior or quantitatively using the pH scale, which spans from 0 to 14 in SI-dimensionless units.
steps: When you taste a lemon or use soap to wash your hands, you are interacting directly with acids and bases in your daily routine.
To begin understanding these substances, observe how they interact with common items in your kitchen and bathroom, such as vinegar, baking soda, and tap water.
Building upon your earlier knowledge of natural indicators, you can test these materials to see how their properties affect everyday tasks like cleaning, digestion, and agriculture.
The key principle here is recognizing that chemical properties dictate practical utility in our homes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer here reveals a misunderstanding of basic household substances, confusing alkaline cleaning agents with acidic food items. Lemon juice contains citric acid, giving it a sour taste and acidic properties.

cards.title: Olfactory indicators are substances whose odor changes or disappears in acidic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Olfactory indicators are substances whose odor changes or disappears in acidic or basic media, allowing us to detect whether a given solution is an acid or a base through our sense of smell. There is no standard physical formula or SI unit for olfactory indicators, as their action relies on chemical properties and sensory perception rather than measurable physical quantities.
steps: Imagine walking into a kitchen where onions are being sliced or vanilla essence is being added to a cake—the distinct, strong aromas are immediately noticeable.
In Class 6, you learned how to test substances with natural indicators like turmeric and China rose by observing color changes.
But what if we used our sense of smell instead of our eyes?
Olfactory indicators work because certain volatile scent molecules react differently when mixed with acids or bases.
To begin exploring this, you will extract or prepare a scent sample and test it by adding drops of common household acids like lemon juice and bases like soap solution.
We will connect this sensory observation method to the concept of indicators studied previously, noting how chemical changes can affect our senses.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer usually confuses olfactory indicators with visual indicators like litmus or turmeric, which change color instead of smell. Students need to remember that "olfactory" relates to the sense of smell.

cards.title: Testing household substances with indicators is the process of using chemical…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Testing household substances with indicators is the process of using chemical color-changing substances to classify everyday materials as acidic, basic, or neutral. There is no single SI unit for this qualitative testing method, as it measures the presence of chemical properties through visible color shifts rather than a physical quantity.
steps: When you squeeze a lemon into water or watch soap suds wash down the kitchen drain, you are interacting with acids and bases in everyday life.
To begin investigating these substances safely, we use special dyes called indicators that change color depending on what they touch.
This builds directly on our understanding of physical observations and recording data from nature.
By preparing natural indicator extracts from items like turmeric or red cabbage, we can systematically test unknown kitchen liquids.
The key principle relies on distinct, reproducible color transitions that reliably reveal the hidden chemical nature of household materials.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer often reveals the misconception that indicators change the temperature or physical state of the substance instead of acting as chemical probes.
